1044.title: Eid around the world
1044.hook: Lebaran in Indonesia, Bayram in Turkey, Sallah in Nigeria
1044.howItsDone: Muslims mark Eid al-Fitr at the end of Ramadan with charity for the poor before the prayer, a congregational prayer in the morning, new or best clothes, family visits and the greeting Eid Mubarak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the musaharati, the drummer who calls each house by name before dawn. Your line was wake for suhur. Who did you wake gently this morning? Day one thousand forty-four.

The month of fasting is over. In Jakarta, the roads out of the city are jammed for days before, as families crowd onto trains, buses and ferries, heading back to the villages they came from. In Istanbul, children are making the rounds of relatives, kissing the hands of their elders and pressing them to their foreheads, and coming away with sweets. In northern Nigeria, horsemen in bright robes and turbans ride in procession before the emir, drums going, crowds cheering. Three countries, three languages, three sets of clothes. One festival. Today: Eid around the world.
screen: `JAKARTA: THE ROADS HOME.` → `ISTANBUL: KISSING THE ELDERS' HANDS.` → `NIGERIA: HORSEMEN BEFORE THE EMIR.`

segments.voice: First, the two days. A hadith recorded by Abu Dawud tells that when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina, the people there had two days a year for games and play. He told them God had given them two better days instead: the day of sacrifice, Eid al-Adha, and the day of breaking the fast, Eid al-Fitr. Today we're mostly with the second, the Eid that ends Ramadan. Second, why it's a celebration at all. The Qur'an, speaking of the fast, says it is so that, in Pickthall's words, "ye should magnify Allah for having guided you, and that peradventure ye may be thankful." The festival is gratitude out loud: the takbir sung on the way to prayer, God is greater, over and over. Third, the names. In Indonesia, Eid is called Lebaran, and the season is known for going home and for asking forgiveness: people say to each other a phrase that asks pardon for any wrong, outward or inward. In Turkey it's Bayram, and Ramazan Bayramı is also called Şeker Bayramı, the sugar holiday, for the sweets. In Nigeria, in Hausa, it's Sallah, and in some northern cities the celebration includes a durbar, a grand procession of horsemen. Fourth, what's the same. Before the Eid prayer, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says, a small charity, a measure of dates or barley, zakat al-fitr, is to be given. Then prayer together in the morning, best clothes, visits, food. And one greeting is heard in many countries: Eid Mubarak. A blessed Eid.
screen: `TWO BETTER DAYS.` · `MAGNIFY ALLAH, AND BE THANKFUL.` · `LEBARAN, BAYRAM, SALLAH.` · `CHARITY FIRST, THEN PRAYER.` · then, large: `EID MUBARAK.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one Eid greeting, and give it a face. Settle, and breathe. Say it once, quietly: Eid Mubarak. Blessed Eid. Let it sit on your tongue. Now think of someone you might say it to, next Eid or the next time it comes around: a neighbor, a coworker, a friend, a shopkeeper you see every week. Picture their face when they hear it. If you're Muslim, think of someone in your family you'd like to visit, or to ask forgiveness from, a Lebaran custom in Indonesia. If you pray, you can give thanks for being guided. The bell holds the time.
Eid around the world. Lebaran in Indonesia, Bayram in Turkey, Sallah in Nigeria: one festival of thanks after the fast, in many languages. Today's word.
Your line: eid in every language. Today, look up how Eid is greeted in one language you don't speak, and say it out loud once. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: The Hajj caravans
1045.hook: caravans from Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad carried pilgrims and the new cover for the Ka'ba
1045.howItsDone: Today pilgrims travel to Mecca in organized groups, by air, sea or road, often led by a guide, which carries on the caravan's habit of making the journey together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid around the world: Lebaran, Bayram, Sallah, and one greeting, Eid Mubarak. Your line was eid in every language. Which greeting did you learn? Day one thousand forty-five.

Bells first, then dust. A long line of camels sways out under a city gate before sunrise, bells at their necks. Curtained litters on their backs, riders swaying inside. Water skins, sacks of grain, guards on horseback, a doctor, a judge, merchants hoping to trade along the way. People line the road to watch them go, some in tears, because the road is long and hard. Some days back we stood in a terminal at Jeddah, with pilgrims a day from home. Before the planes and the ships, this is how the Hajj began. Today: the Hajj caravans.
screen: `BELLS, THEN DUST.` → `OUT OF THE CITY GATE.` → `BEFORE THE PLANES.`

segments.voice: First, the duty and its condition. At the Jeddah terminal we heard the verse that makes the pilgrimage owed "for him who can find a way thither." Then the way was a flight. Here, look at what the same words asked of a pilgrim in the caravan centuries: finding a way meant a road, and a road meant company. You did not cross the desert alone. Second, the great cities. Caravans gathered in Cairo, in Damascus, in Baghdad, and set out together on fixed routes. A caravan was led by an appointed commander of the pilgrimage, the amir al-hajj, whose job was to keep the people fed, watered, guarded, and moving. The traveler Ibn Battuta, from Morocco, wrote of going to Mecca with the caravan from Damascus. Third, the road itself. Along the route from Iraq ran a line of wells and cisterns, and tradition credits Zubayda, the wife of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, whom we met earlier this year, with paying for many of them, so the road still carries her name. Water, in the desert, was the gift that let a pilgrim live to pray. Fourth, what rode along. From Cairo and Damascus, a richly decorated empty litter, the mahmal, traveled with the caravan as a sign of the ruler's care for the pilgrims. And from Cairo, the caravan carried something for the House itself, a new cloth for the Ka'ba. More on that tomorrow. The Qur'an pictures pilgrims coming on foot and on lean camels, "from every deep ravine." Behind each of those ravines was a road, and people who kept it open.
screen: `FOR HIM WHO CAN FIND A WAY.` · `CAIRO, DAMASCUS, BAGHDAD.` · `ZUBAYDA'S WELLS ON THE ROAD.` · `THE MAHMAL AND A NEW CLOTH.` · then, large: `THE LONG ROAD TO MECCA.`

segments.voice: The practice: travel the long road in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture yourself at a city gate before sunrise, your bags tied on a camel. Feel the first hour, the slow sway, the sun coming up over sand. Then the long middle: heat, thirst, a well at evening, strangers becoming companions around a fire. Don't hurry it. Notice how far it is, step after step. Then, at last, someone up ahead calls out, and the road bends toward Mecca. If you pray, you can remember everyone who ever walked that road, and those who never arrived. If not, simply honor the distance. The bell holds the time.
The Hajj caravans. Companies of pilgrims setting out from Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad, led by an amir al-hajj, carrying people and a new cloth for the Ka'ba. Today's word.
Your line: the long road to mecca. Today, on any slow stretch, a commute, a queue, a long walk, remember the caravans and travel it without complaint. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: The kiswah
1046.hook: the black cloth with gold verses is renewed each year at Hajj
1046.carry: a new cloth for the house
1046.howItsDone: Once a year a new kiswah, made in Mecca from black silk with Qur'anic verses in gold and silver thread, is hung on the Ka'ba, and pieces of the old cloth are given as gifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hajj caravans out of Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad, with Zubayda's wells along the way. Your line was the long road to mecca. Which slow stretch did you walk without complaint? Day one thousand forty-six.

In a workshop, a craftsman bends over a stretched length of black silk. His needle carries gold-colored thread. Stitch by stitch, a letter rises off the cloth, raised and shining, part of a line of the Qur'an. Beside him another worker is on a different letter of the same word. Nobody here is making a garment for a person. They are dressing a building, a plain cube of stone in Mecca that people around the world turn toward every day. The black seen in photographs of the Ka'ba is not its wall. It's a garment. Today's word: kiswah.
screen: `BLACK SILK, GOLD THREAD.` → `DRESSING A BUILDING.` → `NOT THE WALL: A GARMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Kiswah is the Arabic word for clothing, a garment. The Ka'ba's walls are stone; the kiswah is what it wears. Second, the House it covers. The Qur'an remembers Abraham and the House, and says, in Pickthall's words, that God made the House "a resort for mankind and a sanctuary." A place people return to. The kiswah honors that House the way a family might set out its best cloth for a guest. Third, an old custom. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Aisha, the Prophet's wife, says that before the fast of Ramadan was made a duty, people fasted on a certain day, and that was the day the Ka'ba was covered. So the covering is older than the Ramadan fast. For a long stretch of later history, the new cloth was made in Egypt and traveled to Mecca with the Cairo caravan we followed yesterday, greeted in the streets as it left. Today it's made in Mecca itself, in a workshop set up for that one task. Fourth, the renewal. Once a year a new kiswah is hung and the old one comes down. Tradition says the old cloth is cut into pieces and given away, and some of those pieces end up framed on walls in homes and museums far from Mecca. Look closely at the gold band near the top, and you'll see verses of the Qur'an worked in thread, and lower down, panels of calligraphy around the door. A cube of stone, given a new garment every year. A new cloth for the house.
screen: `KISWAH: A GARMENT FOR THE HOUSE.` · `A RESORT FOR MANKIND AND A SANCTUARY.` · `COVERED BEFORE RAMADAN'S FAST.` · `HUNG NEW, ONCE A YEAR.` · then, large: `A NEW CLOTH FOR THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the calligraphy. If you can, find a close photo of the kiswah, especially the gold band or the door curtain. If not, picture it: black cloth, a band of gold letters running around the cube. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to read every word. Follow one stroke with your eyes, from where it starts to where it curls and ends. Then another. Notice how the lines lean together, how the gold sits up off the black. Somebody stitched each of those curves by hand. If you pray, you can let one verse you know rise in your mind. If not, simply admire the patience. The bell holds the time.
Kiswah. The garment of the Ka'ba, black cloth with verses in gold thread, renewed once a year. Today's word.
Your line: a new cloth for the house. Today, freshen one thing in a place where people gather, a tablecloth, a cushion, a clean towel by the sink, as a small act of honor. Day one thousand forty-six.

1047.title: Ashura remembered
1047.hook: Sunnis fast for Musa's rescue; Shia mourn Husayn; some keep both
1047.howItsDone: On the tenth of Muharram, Sunni Muslims who keep the day fast, following the Prophet's practice, some adding the ninth; Shia communities hold mourning gatherings for Husayn, recite elegies, and some set up stands giving free water in memory of his thirst.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kiswah, the black cloth with its gold verses, sewn and hung on the Ka'ba at Hajj. Your line was a new cloth for the house. What did you freshen or mend for someone else? Day one thousand forty-seven.

A folding table on a street corner. A big steel cooler, a stack of paper cups, and someone pouring water for every stranger who walks by, no questions, no charge. In some Shia neighborhoods, on the tenth of the month of Muharram, tables like this appear. A few streets away, someone else hasn't eaten since before dawn. They're fasting, and they'll break the fast at sunset. Same day. Same calendar page. The cup remembers a thirst on the plain of Karbala. The fast remembers a rescue at the sea. And some people, quietly, keep both. Today: Ashura remembered.
screen: `A CUP OF WATER ON A STREET CORNER.` → `A FAST UNTIL SUNSET.` → `ONE DAY, TWO MEMORIES.`

segments.voice: Ashura means the tenth, the tenth day of Muharram, the first month of the year. Start with the rescue. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina and found the Jews there fasting on this day. He asked why. They said it was the day God saved Musa and his people from Pharaoh, and Musa fasted it in thanks. The Prophet said he had more right to Musa than they, and he fasted it, and told his community to fast. So the first meaning of the day is gratitude for a sea that opened. Then the grief. Years after the Prophet's death, on this same tenth, his grandson Husayn was killed at Karbala with his family and companions, cut off from the river, thirsty. We told that day in full earlier this year. For Shia Muslims, Ashura became the heart of the year's mourning: gatherings, elegies, the story read aloud again. The water tables remember his thirst. Third, the two together. Sunni Muslims keep the fast from the Prophet's practice, and they honor Husayn as the Prophet's grandson. Some fast and grieve on the same day. Shia scholars have their own views on fasting that day, and they differ. Nobody needs to rank the memories to hold them. Fourth, look back at this whole stretch: lanterns, a cannon, a drummer before dawn, Eid in many languages, caravans, a new cloth for the Ka'ba, and now a cup of water. Holy days survived the centuries the way this one does, in small things people do with their hands.
screen: `ASHURA: THE TENTH OF MUHARRAM.` · `A FAST FOR MUSA'S RESCUE AT THE SEA.` · `MOURNING FOR HUSAYN'S THIRST AT KARBALA.` · `SOME KEEP BOTH ON ONE DAY.` · then: `HOLY DAYS LIVE IN SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: The practice: water. If you have a glass nearby, fill it, or simply hold your hands as if you were holding one. Settle, and breathe. Think of the sea opening for people who were sure they were trapped. Then think of a camp by a river, where the water was kept from them. Rescue, and grief. Hold the glass a moment without drinking, remembering a camp that had no water to drink, and let both be true at once. Then drink, or breathe, slowly. Then think of one person today you could hand a drink to, a coworker, a stranger, someone at home. If you pray, you can say the line the Qur'an gives for loss: we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning. The bell holds the time.
Ashura remembered. The tenth of Muharram: a fast of thanks for Musa's rescue, and mourning for Husayn's death at Karbala. Today's word.

Your line: rescue and grief. Today, give someone water, or skip one small comfort and remember someone who went without. Tomorrow a new stretch begins: what the history teaches. Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: Rise and fall
1048.hook: Ibn Khaldun saw that unity builds and comfort loosens
1048.howItsDone: Muslims often speak of the community as one body or one building, and gather for congregational prayer, Friday prayer, family visits and the Eids partly to keep those bonds strong.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashura remembered: a fast for Musa's rescue at the sea, and grief for Husayn's thirst at Karbala. Your line was rescue and grief. Did you hand someone a drink? Day one thousand forty-eight.

A new stretch starts today, and it asks a different question. For a long stretch now this path has walked through history: cities founded, caliphs crowned, libraries filled, armies at the gates, dynasties that came in from the desert and dynasties that faded out in palaces. Names, places, reigns. Now step back from the map. What does all of it teach? Not about kings. About people, and about a faith carried through time. The first lesson comes from a scholar we've already met, the one who was lowered down a city wall on ropes to talk with a conqueror. Today: rise and fall.
screen: `A NEW STRETCH: WHAT THE HISTORY TEACHES.` → `STEP BACK FROM THE MAP.`

segments.voice: Ibn Khaldun, the historian of Tunis, looked at the dynasties of North Africa and saw a pattern. A group bound tightly together, by kinship, hardship and loyalty, gains the strength to build. Then comfort settles in, the next generations inherit power without the struggle that made it, and the bond loosens. He called that bond asabiyya. We met the idea earlier this year. Today, hold it up against everything since. Go back through the stories: a movement rises from the Sahara or the mountains, sure of itself and of each other, and builds. A court grows splendid, and its rivals grow inside the walls. Ibn Khaldun wrote of it almost like a life span, as natural to dynasties as age is to a person. He didn't call it a punishment. Read today, it works as a warning. Second, the Qur'an names the bond in its own way. In Pickthall's translation: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." The image is a rope, gripped by many hands at once. Let go one by one, and nobody notices at first. Third, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari pictures believers as a building, each part holding up the others, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, laced his fingers together to show it. Fourth, the small scale. A family, a mosque, a group of friends, a team at work: each rises when people show up for one another, and drifts when everyone gets comfortable enough not to. Comfort isn't a sin. Nobody is told to live in a tent. But bonds that aren't tended loosen on their own.
screen: `ASABIYYA: THE BOND THAT BUILDS.` · `HOLD FAST TO THE ROPE TOGETHER.` · `BELIEVERS LIKE ONE BUILDING.` · `FAMILIES AND TEAMS RISE AND DRIFT TOO.` · then, large: `AND DO NOT SEPARATE.`

segments.voice: The practice: strengthen one bond. Settle, and breathe. Lace your fingers together the way the Prophet did, and feel how each hand holds the other. Now think of one bond in your life that has gone slack. A cousin you only see at weddings. A friend from an old job. A neighbor whose name you never learned. Don't solve the whole relationship. Just choose one small thing that would pull the rope a little tighter: a message, a visit, a question about their day. Hold that person in mind until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Rise and fall. Ibn Khaldun's pattern: a bond builds a people up, and comfort loosens it. Today's word.
Your line: unity builds. Today, send the message or make the visit you chose, before the evening gets comfortable. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: Knowledge was worship
1049.hook: scholars studied the stars and the body for the sake of Allah
1049.howItsDone: Muslims often begin study with the name of God and a renewed intention, and the Qur'an's plea for more knowledge (20:114) is one some students say before a lesson.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rise and fall: Ibn Khaldun's pattern, a bond that builds and comfort that loosens. Your line was unity builds. Did you pull one rope a little tighter? Day one thousand forty-nine.

Standing. Sitting. Lying on your side. The Qur'an describes people who remember God in all three positions, and then it adds one more thing they do: they consider the creation of the heavens and the earth. Remembering, and then looking hard at the world. Put side by side in one verse. Back through this year's history we've met astronomers, physicians, mapmakers, people who measured the sky and opened books on the eye. It's easy to file them under science, a different drawer from prayer. The verse doesn't seem to keep two drawers. Today: knowledge was worship.
screen: `STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN.` → `THEN: CONSIDER THE CREATION.` → `ONE DRAWER, NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse itself, near the close of the third surah. The people of understanding remember Allah standing, sitting and reclining, they consider the heavens and the earth, and what comes out of their mouths is praise. In Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." The study ends in worship. Second, the body. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet, peace be upon him, saying that God has not sent down a disease without sending down its cure. Some readers heard that as a promise and an assignment at once: the cure exists, so go and find it. Physicians in Muslim lands wrote on the eye, on fevers, on the heart, and some of them saw the search as service. Third, the same person. History keeps handing us people who don't fit one label. Ibn Rushd of Cordoba was a judge of Islamic law and a physician. Ibn Sina wrote a canon of medicine and also commentaries on chapters of the Qur'an. To them the line between a religious subject and a worldly one wasn't drawn where a modern school timetable draws it. Fourth, the intention. What turned study into worship wasn't the subject. A scholar of grammar could study for fame; a pharmacist could study for God. The tradition kept asking what the work was for. That's the lesson the history leaves on an ordinary desk: a spreadsheet, a textbook, an engine manual. Look hard enough, with the right reason, and the verse's last line is waiting at the end.
screen: `REMEMBER, CONSIDER, THEN PRAISE.` · `EVERY DISEASE HAS A CURE: GO FIND IT.` · `A JUDGE WHO WAS ALSO A PHYSICIAN.` · `THE INTENTION MAKES IT WORSHIP.` · then, large: `THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: study something for Him, or simply for its own sake if that's how you come to it. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing within reach and look at it the way an astronomer looks at a star. Your own hand works well. The lines across the palm, the joints, the pulse at the wrist you can feel with two fingers. Count nothing. Just look closer than you usually would, and notice how much is there that you didn't make. If you pray, you can end with the verse's own words: our Lord, You did not create this in vain. The bell holds the time.
Knowledge was worship. Studying the stars and the body, with the right intention, as a way of turning toward God. Today's word.
Your line: study as prayer. Today, learn one real thing about how the body or the sky works, and before you start, say to yourself what it's for. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: The ordinary believer
1050.hook: history is kings, but faith was carried by mothers, farmers and traders
1050.howItsDone: Muslims often learn their first surahs and the prayer from parents and grandparents at home, and some pray for the forgiveness of their teachers and parents by name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, knowledge was worship: the stars and the body studied, with the right intention, as a way of turning to God. Your line was study as prayer. What did you learn, and what was it for? Day one thousand fifty.

In Medina, in the Prophet's mosque, someone used to sweep the floor. The narrator of the hadith isn't even sure whether it was a man or a woman. One day the Prophet, peace be upon him, noticed the sweeper was missing and asked. People told him the sweeper had died and been buried. They hadn't thought it worth telling him. He asked them to show him the grave, and he went and prayed there. A sweeper whose name the record didn't keep, and a prophet who walked to the grave. Today: the ordinary believer.
screen: `SOMEONE SWEPT THE MOSQUE.` → `BURIED, UNNOTICED.` → `HE WENT TO THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: First, notice what that story in Sahih al-Bukhari keeps and what it drops. It keeps the work and the visit. It drops the name. Second, look at who the chronicles name. Caliphs, sultans, generals, the occasional famous scholar. That's what chroniclers wrote down. But a faith doesn't survive on coronations. Someone had to teach a child the opening surah at a kitchen table. Someone had to stop work at the edge of a field when the time for prayer came. Someone had to carry the prayer across the sea in a trader's head, and keep it in a port town far from home. Mothers, farmers, traders, sweepers. Mostly unnamed. Third, the tradition itself points the light at them. A hadith in Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet saying that God does not look at your bodies or your appearance, but at your hearts and your deeds. Not your title. Not your wealth. Fourth, take that lens back through the reigns this path has named. The bond Ibn Khaldun wrote about lives or dies in ordinary friendships. Even yesterday's scholars learned their first letters from someone. Every time this path told you a ruler's name, there were unnamed people under that reign, raising children, working fields, teaching the prayer. The history books are thin on them. The faith isn't.
screen: `THE SWEEPER OF THE MOSQUE.` · `CHRONICLES NAME THE KINGS.` · `GOD LOOKS AT HEARTS AND DEEDS.` · `UNDER EVERY REIGN, UNNAMED HANDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank an ordinary believer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who passed something good on to you, and who will never be in a history book. Whoever taught you a prayer, or how to be kind, or how to keep going. A grandparent, a teacher, an aunt, a neighbor, a coach. See their face, their hands, the room where it happened. Stay with them until the bell. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for them by name. If they're living, decide how you'll tell them. The bell holds the time.
The ordinary believer. The unnamed mothers, farmers, traders and sweepers who carried the faith while the chronicles wrote about kings. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary hands carried it. Today, thank one person who passed something on to you, out loud or in writing. Day one thousand fifty.

what it means: the faith was carried by unnamed mothers, farmers, traders and sweepers.
